inputs.need:
I am the vascular access nurse specialist at a 520-bed teaching hospital. On 1 March 2025 we changed our peripheral intravenous catheter policy on the adult medical and surgical wards from routine resiting every 96 hours to replacement only when clinically indicated, with a documented site assessment every shift using a phlebitis score. The change followed complaints from patients about repeated cannulation and a push from the wards to save nursing time.

Since then I hear two stories. Some ward nurses say they are seeing more phlebitis and more infiltration because catheters now stay in for a week or longer. Others say patients get far fewer painful reinsertions and that nothing bad has happened. Infection prevention has recorded two bloodstream infections linked to peripheral catheters since the change, against one in the year before, and that has worried our nursing executive.

I want to design a cohort study comparing catheters inserted in the 12 months before the policy change with catheters inserted in the 12 months after. The main outcome I have in mind is catheter failure, meaning removal for phlebitis, infiltration, occlusion or dislodgement before the end of treatment. I would also like to look at the number of catheters per admission, dwell time and bloodstream infections, although I know infections are rare. Insertion date, site, gauge, removal date and removal reason are documented in the vascular access flowsheet in our electronic health record, and infection prevention keeps its own line infection surveillance list.

I need help with the comparison, how to handle the fact that one patient can have several catheters, what to do about secular trends and other changes on the wards, and how many catheters we need.
inputs.constraints: Secondary use of existing flowsheet and surveillance data only; no new data collection from patients. The clinical informatics team can give about 30 hours for data extraction. The nursing executive wants results by June 2027.
localFacts: The clinically indicated replacement policy took effect on all adult medical and surgical wards on 1 March 2025; the previous policy required resiting every 96 hours.
The vascular access flowsheet records insertion date and time, site, gauge, inserter role, removal date and time, and removal reason for each peripheral catheter.
Infection prevention recorded two peripheral catheter-associated bloodstream infections from March 2025 to February 2026 and one in the 12 months before.
The research ethics board approved secondary use of flowsheet and surveillance data for this evaluation with a waiver of consent on 2026-08-27 (REB-2026-0412).
The clinical informatics manager agreed to provide about 30 hours of extraction and linkage time for this evaluation (request CI-2026-117).

steps.note: The need names one design (cohort), so classifyFamily in src/lib/stages.ts at 875fe59 routes it as explicit cohort. design.basis 'explicit' at create requires S11.

response.title: Peripheral intravenous catheter failure before and after a change to clinically indicated replacement
response.subtitle: Cohort from existing flowsheet and surveillance data, adult medical and surgical wards
response.statement: On 1 March 2025 the hospital replaced routine resiting of peripheral intravenous catheters every 96 hours with replacement only when clinically indicated. Ward nurses disagree about whether longer dwell has brought more phlebitis and infiltration, and the nursing executive is concerned about bloodstream infections. A cohort comparing catheters inserted in the 12 months before and after the change will estimate whether catheter failure increased, and by how much insertions per admission fell.
response.whoAffected: Adults on the medical and surgical wards who need peripheral intravenous therapy, the ward nurses who insert and assess catheters, and the nursing executive and infection prevention team who own the policy.
response.whatHurts: A failed catheter interrupts treatment and means another painful insertion; a policy that raised failure would harm patients, while a return to routine resiting would bring back unnecessary insertions if the concern is unfounded.
response.currentPractice: Catheters stay in place while functioning and clinically needed, with a phlebitis score documented every shift; the removal reason is recorded in the vascular access flowsheet.
response.whyNow: Twelve months of data after the change now exist, the nursing executive wants an answer by June 2027, and ethics approval for secondary use is in place.
response.constraints: Secondary use of existing flowsheet and surveillance data only; no new data collection from patients. The clinical informatics team can give about 30 hours for data extraction. The nursing executive wants results by June 2027.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients receive intravenous treatment with as few insertions as possible and without more catheter failure or infection.
response.summary: Problem framed as a before-after cohort of catheters from existing records, with catheter failure as the main outcome.

records.title: Clinically indicated versus routine replacement of peripheral intravenous catheters after a policy change: a before-after cohort on four surgical wards
records.authors: Adebayo-Lindqvist T, Moreau-Kaplan S, Hughes-Oyelowo R
records.abstract: Four surgical wards changed from routine replacement of peripheral intravenous catheters every 72 hours to replacement only when clinically indicated. We compared 2,310 catheters inserted in the six months before the change with 2,188 catheters inserted in the six months after. Catheter failure, defined as removal for phlebitis, infiltration, occlusion or dislodgement before the end of treatment, occurred in 31 percent of catheters before and 33 percent after. Median dwell time rose from 58 to 81 hours, and the number of catheters inserted per 100 patient-days fell from 36 to 27. Phlebitis was recorded for 6 percent of catheters in both periods. The comparison used ward records without adjustment for patient mix or for other changes on the wards.

records.title: Monthly catheter failure before and after a switch to clinically indicated replacement: an interrupted time series in a general hospital
records.abstract: A general hospital switched all adult wards from routine replacement of peripheral catheters every 72 hours to clinically indicated replacement. We plotted the monthly proportion of catheters removed for failure for 18 months before and 18 months after the switch and fitted a segmented regression. Failure was 28 percent in the month before the switch, and there was no step change at the switch (0.9 percentage points, 95 percent confidence interval -2.1 to 3.9) and no change in slope. A change of catheter brand eight months after the switch coincided with a short rise in occlusions. The analysis used ward-level monthly counts and could not account for patients with several catheters.

records.title: Shift-by-shift phlebitis scoring and catheter dwell beyond 96 hours on medical wards: an observational study
records.authors: Oyelaran-Castaneda B, Lindgren-Adu P, Whitcombe-Sato K
records.abstract: After the hospital adopted clinically indicated replacement, nurses on three medical wards scored insertion sites every shift with a five-point phlebitis scale. Of 1,694 catheters, 431 stayed in place beyond 96 hours. The rate of phlebitis did not rise with dwell beyond 96 hours: 4.1 per 1,000 catheter-days up to 96 hours and 3.8 per 1,000 catheter-days afterwards. Site assessment was documented in 83 percent of shifts, and documentation was least complete at night and at weekends. Catheters with incomplete site documentation were more often removed for infiltration. The study could not examine bloodstream infection because only two occurred.

records.title: Routine resiting and the pain of repeated insertion in adult medical inpatients: a two-hospital cohort
records.abstract: We followed 406 adult medical inpatients with a peripheral intravenous catheter at two hospitals, one with a policy of routine resiting every 96 hours and one replacing catheters only when clinically indicated. Patients at the routine resiting hospital had a median of three insertions per admission, against two at the other hospital. Patients rated the pain of each observed insertion on a scale from 0 to 10; 38 percent of patients at the routine resiting hospital reported at least one insertion scored 7 or higher, against 24 percent at the other hospital. Catheter failure was similar at the two hospitals. Patient mix differed between the hospitals, and pain was recorded only for insertions that a research nurse observed.

records.title: Infiltration with longer peripheral catheter dwell in inpatients aged 75 and over: an observational study on two medical wards
records.abstract: We followed 812 peripheral catheters in patients aged 75 and over on two medical wards that used clinically indicated replacement. Infiltration occurred in 14 percent of catheters and became more frequent after the fourth day of dwell (hazard ratio 1.6 for each further day, 95 percent confidence interval 1.2 to 2.1). Most infiltrations were found at the scheduled site check rather than reported by patients, and infiltrations in patients with delirium were found later than in other patients. Phlebitis was uncommon. The two wards had higher nurse staffing than the hospital average, which may limit how far the findings apply.

After moves to clinically indicated replacement, catheter failure was similar in an unadjusted before-after cohort (31 and 33 percent) and showed no step change in an interrupted time series, insertions per patient fell, and phlebitis did not rise with dwell beyond 96 hours on wards that scored sites every shift. records.title: Clinically indicated replacement of peripheral intravenous catheters in adults: a systematic review of catheter failure, phlebitis and bloodstream infection
records.authors: Delacroix-Mensah L, Nakamura-Pike J, Oduya-Fraser C, Brennan-Soto R
records.abstract: We searched five databases to June 2020 for trials and cohort studies comparing clinically indicated with routine replacement of peripheral intravenous catheters in adults. The review included 9 trials and 11 cohort studies. In the trials, phlebitis and bloodstream infection did not differ between the two strategies, and clinically indicated replacement led to fewer insertions per patient. The cohort studies reported more variable results: catheter failure was higher after a policy change in 3 of 11. Few studies accounted for patients who had several catheters, and most cohort studies did not adjust for changes in patient mix over time.

records.title: Peripheral catheter-associated bloodstream infection by dwell time in adult inpatients: a surveillance cohort from six hospitals
records.authors: Rutherford-Mbeki A, Kowalczyk-Obi D, Tanaka-Holm E
records.abstract: Six hospitals reported peripheral catheter-associated bloodstream infections through a shared surveillance system for three years, covering about 214,000 peripheral catheters. The infection rate was 0.08 per 1,000 catheter-days overall. Rates were similar for catheters in place up to 96 hours and for catheters in place longer, but catheters inserted in the emergency department had about twice the rate of catheters inserted on the wards. Staphylococcus aureus caused most infections. Only 58 infections occurred in total, so the estimates by dwell time were imprecise, and the hospitals used different replacement policies during the period.

records.title: Accounting for several catheters per patient in analyses of peripheral intravenous catheter failure: a methodological case study
records.abstract: Using 6,120 peripheral catheters from 2,874 adult admissions, we compared analyses of catheter failure that treated catheters as independent with analyses that accounted for several catheters per patient. The analysis that ignored clustering gave a hazard ratio of 1.24 for dwell beyond 96 hours, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.08 to 1.42, while a shared frailty model gave 1.12, with an interval of 0.93 to 1.35. Patients with many catheters were sicker and contributed a disproportionate share of failures. We recommend patient-level clustering in every analysis of catheter failure and reporting the number of catheters per patient.

records.title: Removal reasons for peripheral intravenous catheters in the electronic flowsheet: completeness and agreement with bedside observation
records.abstract: We compared the removal reason recorded in the electronic flowsheet with the reason observed by a research nurse at the bedside for 540 peripheral catheter removals on four wards. A removal reason was missing for 11 percent of removals. Where a reason was recorded, it agreed with the observed reason for 86 percent of removals; disagreement was most common between infiltration and occlusion and between end of treatment and dislodgement. Removals on night shifts more often lacked a reason. We recommend a fixed list of removal reasons and a check of free-text entries before any analysis of catheter failure.

records.title: Nursing time for peripheral catheter care before and after a change to clinically indicated replacement: a time-motion study
records.abstract: Trained observers timed peripheral catheter tasks on two medical wards for four weeks before and four weeks after a change from routine resiting to clinically indicated replacement. Time spent on insertions fell from 41 to 26 minutes per 10 patients per day, while time spent on site assessment and documentation rose from 12 to 19 minutes. Nurses reported fewer difficult insertions at night. The study did not measure catheter complications, and the observers knew which period they were observing, which may have influenced the timings.

steps.note: Second search, on the questions the first did not cover (infection, analysis of several catheters per patient, removal-reason documentation, nursing time): five more records, appended after the first five. response.synthesis: Ten retrieved records from two searches, appraised at abstract level. After moves to clinically indicated replacement, catheter failure was similar in a before-after cohort (31 and 33 percent) and in an interrupted time series, but higher after a policy change in 3 of 11 cohort studies in a systematic review whose 9 trials found no difference in phlebitis or bloodstream infection and fewer insertions. Phlebitis did not rise with dwell beyond 96 hours where sites were scored every shift, while infiltration rose after the fourth day in patients aged 75 and over. Ignoring several catheters per patient inflated a dwell effect from 1.12 to 1.24. Bloodstream infection is rare (0.08 per 1,000 catheter-days); flowsheet removal reasons were missing for 11 percent of removals in one validation; nursing time moved from insertion to site assessment.
response.gradeRationale: Overall certainty is not rated across these records: they address different outcomes with different designs, and one label would hide that. Per outcome: catheter failure after a policy change, low (observational comparisons with inconsistent results); phlebitis, low; infiltration in older patients, low; bloodstream infection, very low (few events, imprecise); insertions per patient, moderate (consistent in trials).
response.summary: Ten retrieved records appraised; six source-derived claims; no single overall certainty, with certainty stated per outcome in the rationale.

response.reading: The policy acts through dwell time: catheters stay longer, fewer are inserted, and shift-by-shift site assessment carries the safety load. The retrieved records show little change in failure and no rise in phlebitis with longer dwell where sites are scored, but infiltration rises after the fourth day in older patients and documentation weakens at night and at weekends. Patients who need many catheters are sicker and dominate failures, so the unit of analysis matters. Bloodstream infection worries the executive but is too rare to compare locally.

response.rationale: The exposure (insertion before or after 1 March 2025) and the outcome (removal reason) are recorded for every catheter, so a cohort of all catheters on both sides of the change answers the executive's question directly. Retrieved comparisons found little change in failure after similar policies (c1, c3) and no rise in phlebitis with longer dwell where sites are scored every shift (c2), so the local study must be precise enough to rule out a meaningful rise; it must also account for several catheters per patient, which changed a dwell estimate materially (c4). A monthly time series within the same data guards against secular trends.
alternatives: Cluster randomised comparison of replacement policies between wards (refused: the policy is already hospital-wide and reversing it on some wards for a trial is not proposed)
Ward-level interrupted time series only (kept as a secondary analysis: it cannot adjust for patient-level differences)
Prospective observation of new catheters for three months (refused: slower, and the constraint is secondary use of existing data)
response.whyNotMoreComplex: A trial would answer a question the published trials have largely answered; the local question is whether the policy as delivered on these wards changed failure, which existing records can answer within the executive's timeline.

decision.statement: Run the cohort comparing catheters inserted in the 12 months before and after 1 March 2025, built from existing flowsheet and surveillance data, with catheter failure as the primary outcome, several catheters per patient accounted for, and a monthly time series to separate the policy from secular trends.
decision.question: Should the question about the clinically indicated replacement policy be answered with a before-after cohort from existing records?

response.overview: Cohort of all peripheral intravenous catheters inserted on adult medical and surgical wards from 1 March 2024 to 28 February 2026, comparing the 12 months after the change to clinically indicated replacement with the 12 months before, built from existing flowsheet and infection surveillance data.
response.population: Catheters inserted on adult medical and surgical wards in patients aged 18 and over; catheters inserted in the emergency department or operating theatres are excluded from the primary analysis and described separately; catheters without a removal record at discharge are counted and handled in a sensitivity analysis.
response.exposure: Insertion from 1 March 2025 to 28 February 2026 (after the change) versus 1 March 2024 to 28 February 2025 (before).
response.procedures: Clinical informatics extracts every eligible flowsheet record and links it to the admission episode and to the infection prevention surveillance list inside the hospital's secure environment; the analysis file carries study identifiers only. Removal reasons are mapped to failure (phlebitis, infiltration, occlusion, dislodgement) or non-failure (end of treatment, discharge, routine resite) with a coding rule fixed before extraction, because flowsheet reasons were missing for 11 percent of removals in a validation study (c6); a second nurse recodes a random 5 percent of free-text reasons. Co-interventions on the wards (staffing changes, new catheter products, education sessions) are listed by month from ward managers' records.

outcomes.name: Catheter failure
outcomes.measure: Removal for phlebitis, infiltration, occlusion or dislodgement before the end of treatment, per catheter

outcomes.name: Catheters per admission
outcomes.measure: Number of peripheral catheters inserted per admission episode
outcomes.why: The benefit the policy was meant to bring and the one patients notice.

outcomes.why: The executive's concern; too rare for a comparison but must be reported.

outcomes.timing: Every shift during dwell; at removal
outcomes.why: The policy relies on assessment every shift, and failure can only be measured where a reason is recorded.

response.feasibility: About 30 hours of clinical informatics time for extraction and linkage (request CI-2026-117); analysis by the investigator with a hospital statistician; results before June 2027.
biasMitigation: Failure coding rule fixed before extraction, with a 5 percent recode by a second nurse
Monthly time series with 12 points on each side and co-interventions annotated
Six covariates fixed before extraction; dwell time not adjusted for because it lies on the causal path of the policy

parsimony.simplestPath: One exposure contrast, one primary outcome, one clustered model and one pre-specified time series.

response.theoreticalFramework: No framework is needed beyond the causal diagram used to choose covariates; the question is a comparison of two policies with routine data.
response.summary: Cohort of catheters on both sides of the policy change; one primary outcome, two secondary outcomes and one process measure, with clustering and secular trends handled by design.

response.designSummary: Cohort of catheters clustered within patients, comparing the 12 months after the change with the 12 months before, with an interrupted time series of monthly failure as the main check on secular trends.
response.sampleSize: If the wards insert about 9,000 catheters a year (an assumption to confirm from the 2024 flowsheet count), about 18,000 catheters are available. With failure near 31 percent before the change, the planning value from c1, detecting a rise to 34 percent (3 percentage points) with 90 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 needs about 5,100 catheters per period if catheters were independent; with a design effect of 1.4 for several catheters per patient, about 7,200 per period. Both periods should exceed this, so the study can detect or rule out a 3-point rise. Bloodstream infection is too rare for a comparison and is reported as counts.
response.primaryAnalysis: Cause-specific Cox model for time from insertion to failure, with removal for other reasons as a competing event and a shared frailty term for the patient (c4), period after versus before as the exposure, adjusted for age, sex, admitting service, insertion site, catheter gauge and inserter role; reported as a hazard ratio and as an absolute difference in 7-day cumulative incidence with 95 percent confidence intervals.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Segmented regression of the monthly proportion of failed catheters with 12 points on each side (level and slope change), as in the retrieved time series (c3); catheters per admission compared with negative binomial regression; bloodstream infections described as counts and rates; documentation completeness described by shift and period.
response.missingData: Catheters without a removal reason are counted by period and analysed in a sensitivity analysis that treats them first as failures and then as non-failures; missing covariates are handled by multiple imputation with 20 imputations.
response.multiplicity: One primary comparison; secondary outcomes are reported with confidence intervals and labelled secondary.
response.software: R with the survival and coxme packages, inside the hospital's secure analysis environment.
overfittingGuards: Six covariates and the failure coding rule fixed before extraction
No adjustment for dwell time in the primary model
Segmented regression specified in advance with 12 points on each side
No subgroup claims beyond the pre-specified age and interpreter-need groups
response.summary: About 7,200 catheters per period are needed for a 3-point difference after clustering; the likely available numbers exceed this.

response.risks: Minimal: secondary use of existing records with no patient contact. The main risks are privacy harm from linkage and blame directed at wards or individual nurses.
response.consent: The research ethics board approved a waiver of consent for secondary use (REB-2026-0412); patients are not contacted.
response.data: Extraction and linkage inside the hospital's secure environment; the analysis file holds study identifiers and month of insertion only; results are reported by service and never by nurse.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older patients, patients with delirium (in whom infiltration was found later in one retrieved study), patients with darker skin, on whom visual phlebitis scoring is less reliable, and patients with limited English, who may not report pain, may be affected differently. Failure is reported by age group and by interpreter need, and the limits of visual scoring are stated.
response.effectiveness: The study tells the executive whether the policy is associated with more catheter failure and how many insertions it saved.
response.efficiency: Uses existing records and about 30 hours of informatics time; no participant contact.
response.costs: Informatics, nursing and statistician time within existing roles; no direct costs.
response.grants: None needed; a clear local result could support a multi-hospital comparison later.
response.partnerships: Infection prevention for surveillance definitions, ward nurse managers for the co-intervention list, clinical informatics, a hospital statistician, and two patient partners from the patient and family advisory council.
response.rebPath: Approved by the hospital research ethics board with a waiver of consent for secondary use (REB-2026-0412), following Declaration of Helsinki principles for research with identifiable data.
response.limitations: A before-after comparison remains open to secular trends; documentation may differ between periods; bloodstream infection is too rare to compare.
response.summary: Minimal-risk secondary use under an approved waiver, with results reported by service and equity groups.

response.partnershipPlan: Two patient partners review the outcome definitions and the plain-language summary; a ward nurse from each service and an infection prevention nurse review the failure coding rule before extraction.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; patient complaints about cannulation from the two years are counted by month as context for the time series.

response.title: Peripheral intravenous catheter failure before and after a change to clinically indicated replacement: a cohort study using routinely collected data
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate whether a change from routine resiting every 96 hours to clinically indicated replacement was associated with more catheter failure on adult medical and surgical wards. Design: cohort of all catheters inserted in the 12 months before and after 1 March 2025, from flowsheet and surveillance records. Outcome: removal for phlebitis, infiltration, occlusion or dislodgement before the end of treatment. Analysis: cause-specific Cox model with a patient frailty term and an interrupted time series. Results and conclusions will be written after the analysis.
response.introduction: Clinically indicated replacement reduces insertions without more phlebitis in published comparisons, but results after local policy changes vary and few analyses account for patients with several catheters. Ward nurses disagree about the effect of the change here, and two bloodstream infections have raised concern.
response.methods: Existing flowsheet records for catheters inserted from 1 March 2024 to 28 February 2026 are linked to admissions and infection surveillance. Removal reasons are coded with a rule fixed in advance and checked on a random sample. The primary model accounts for competing removal and for several catheters per patient; a segmented regression of monthly failure addresses secular trends.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet. The report will present the cohort flow, catheters per patient, failure by period with the adjusted hazard ratio and absolute difference, the monthly time series, catheters per admission, infection counts and documentation completeness.
response.discussion: The discussion will weigh the local estimate against published comparisons, the time series and the co-intervention list, and state what the result means for the policy.
response.limitations: Before-after design open to secular trends; documentation may differ between periods; infections too rare to compare; visual phlebitis scoring.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will be limited to failure and insertions in this hospital and will not claim an effect on bloodstream infection.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am the vascular access nurse specialist at a 520-bed teaching hospital. On 1 March 2025 we changed our peripheral intravenous catheter policy on the adult medical and surgical wards from routine resiting every 96 hours to replacement only when clinically indicated, with a documented site assessment every shift using a phlebitis score. The change followed complaints from patients about repeated cannulation and a push from the wards to save nursing time.

Since then I hear two stories. Some ward nurses say they are seeing more phlebitis and more infiltration because catheters now stay in for a week or longer. Others say patients get far fewer painful reinsertions and that nothing bad has happened. Infection prevention has recorded two bloodstream infections linked to peripheral catheters since the change, against one in the year before, and that has worried our nursing executive.

I want to design a cohort study comparing catheters inserted in the 12 months before the policy change with catheters inserted in the 12 months after. The main outcome I have in mind is catheter failure, meaning removal for phlebitis, infiltration, occlusion or dislodgement before the end of treatment. I would also like to look at the number of catheters per admission, dwell time and bloodstream infections, although I know infections are rare. Insertion date, site, gauge, removal date and removal reason are documented in the vascular access flowsheet in our electronic health record, and infection prevention keeps its own line infection surveillance list.

I need help with the comparison, how to handle the fact that one patient can have several catheters, what to do about secular trends and other changes on the wards, and how many catheters we need.
